newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Limits on Yugoslav vote monitoring unacceptable - EU.
newsitem.headline: Limits on Yugoslav vote monitoring unacceptable - EU.

text.p: The European Union urged Yugoslav authorities on Thursday to let the OSCE monitor elections in the region unfettered, after Belgrade told the organisation it would not allow some OSCE members to take part.

"The EU calls on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (FRY) to accept the (OSCE's) offer of an authentic observation of presidential and legislative elections...," the Luxembourg EU Presidency said in a statement.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said earlier this week it had made Belgrade an offer to monitor and assess the autumn elections in Serbia and Montenegro, which form rump Yugoslavia.
As well as observing the election campaign in the run-up to the voting, it also wanted to check freedom of the media.

"The FRY authorities in their response placed unacceptable limitations on election observation. Their invitation would not allow observation by a number of OSCE countries," it said. The statement was issued by the chairman-in-office of the OSCE, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen.
It did not say which countries were referred to but a Luxembourg government official said the United States was among those told to stay away.

The United States insists the improvement of relations between Washington and Belgrade -- which would help end international financial sanctions against Yugoslavia -- depends in part on more freedom for the press in Serbia.
"The EU refuses the selective approach of the FRY authorities. It invites them to send the OSCE an invitation which has no pre-conditions attached and is not exclusive," the EU presidency added.

It said that in guaranteeing free and democratic elections, "the FRY will show its willingness to choose without ambiguity the way of democracy and of a state of law, and will thus contribute to its complete integration in the international community."
The OSCE said its Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights had an assessment team ready to begin work at 48 hours' notice, should "normal observation standards" be proposed.
